summary: Defines the UIDPLUS extension of IMAP, a set of features that reduce the time and resources used by certain client operations. They are mainly meant for clients that sometimes work offline. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: A shortcut for email programs that lets them keep track of messages with less back-and-forth with the server.

questions: what is the appenduid response code
subtitle: Small IMAP additions that tell a client the UIDs of messages it just copied or appended, and let it expunge only chosen messages.

tldr.problem: Clients that work offline and resynchronize later waste time and risk deleting messages other clients marked as deleted, and they must search to find where copied messages landed.
tldr.mechanism: UIDPLUS adds the UID EXPUNGE command, and the APPENDUID, COPYUID and UIDNOTSTICKY response codes that report the UIDs of new messages or say UIDs are not persistent.
tldr.outcome: These are optimizations: clients can do the same with base IMAP, only less efficiently. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2359.

today: RFC 4315 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2005. It obsoletes RFC 2359, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What UIDPLUS Adds
sections.content:
A server supports the UIDPLUS extension if it returns UIDPLUS in response to the CAPABILITY command. The extension defines one additional command, and it recommends new status response codes that SHOULD be returned by all server implementations, whether or not they implement UIDPLUS.

The features are optimizations. Clients can get equivalent functionality, though less efficiently, using the base protocol. They are primarily intended for disconnected-use clients, which work offline and resynchronize later.
sections.plainLanguage: UIDPLUS gives email programs a few handy shortcuts. They are not required, because the programs could do the same things the slow way.

sections.title: UID EXPUNGE
sections.content:
The UID EXPUNGE command takes a set of UIDs. It permanently removes messages from the selected mailbox only if they both have the \Deleted flag and have a UID in the given set. Everything else is untouched.

This matters for disconnected clients. Plain EXPUNGE removes every message marked \Deleted, including ones that other clients marked while this client was away. UID EXPUNGE avoids that.

If the server lacks UIDPLUS, the client can temporarily clear \Deleted on the messages it wants to keep with STORE, run EXPUNGE, then restore the flag. Or it can use plain EXPUNGE and risk removing messages unintentionally.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain EXPUNGE empties the whole trash can, even things someone else tossed in. UID EXPUNGE empties only the items on your list.

sections.title: APPENDUID, COPYUID and UIDNOTSTICKY
sections.content:
APPENDUID is sent in the tagged OK to an APPEND. It carries the UIDVALIDITY of the destination mailbox and the UID given to the new message. With the MULTIAPPEND extension and several appended messages, the second value is a UID set in transmission order. A UID set form MUST NOT be used for a single message, so a range like 123:123 is forbidden.

COPYUID is sent in the tagged OK to a COPY. It carries the destination UIDVALIDITY, the UIDs of the copied messages in the source, and the UIDs assigned in the destination, in matching order.

UIDNOTSTICKY is sent in an untagged NO response to SELECT. It says the mailbox is on a mail store without persistent UIDs, so UIDVALIDITY differs on each select, and APPEND or COPY will not return APPENDUID or COPYUID. Servers SHOULD NOT have any such mail stores; the facility exists for legacy ones.

If the server does not return these codes, the client can select the destination and find the messages with FETCH or SEARCH, for example by Message-ID.
sections.plainLanguage: After you file a letter in a folder, the folder tells you the number it gave the letter. One special warning means that folder renumbers everything each time you open it, so numbers are useless.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example appends a message to saved-messages and gets [APPENDUID 38505 3955]. Then COPY 2:4 meeting returns [COPYUID 38505 304,319:320 3956:3958], showing which source UIDs became which destination UIDs. A UID COPY 305:310 copies nothing, because the earlier response shows UIDs 305 through 310 do not exist.

Copying to the mailbox funny returns no COPYUID. Selecting it shows [UIDNOTSTICKY] in an untagged NO, which explains why.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows a folder answering "your letters are now numbers 3956 to 3958", and another folder saying it cannot promise any numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: COPYUID and APPENDUID reveal information about a mailbox. That may be sensitive when permissions let a client COPY or APPEND to a mailbox but not SELECT or EXAMINE it. So these codes SHOULD NOT be sent when the client cannot select or examine the mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: If you may drop letters in a box but not look inside, the box should not tell you the numbers of the letters in it.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2359
sections.content:
RFC 4315 obsoletes RFC 2359 but takes substantial text from it, with clarifications. RFC 2359 implied a server must always return COPYUID or APPENDUID data, suggesting arbitrary data when the destination had no persistent UIDs. This document adds UIDNOTSTICKY and says a UIDPLUS server does not return that data when the destination has UIDNOTSTICKY status.

It registers the UIDPLUS capability in the imap4-capabilities registry, replacing RFC 2359.
sections.plainLanguage: The old version could make a server give made-up numbers. The new one adds a clear warning flag instead.
